Chapter 3: Disease in a Fallen World—Theological and Biological Perspectives
Now that we've explored how pathogens can change, let's step back and ask a bigger question—why do we even have diseases in the first place?
If you look through the lens of the biblical narrative, disease isn’t just a random glitch in the system. Instead, it’s deeply tied to the idea of a fallen world—a creation that’s been changed by the weight of human choices.
Picture this: According to Genesis, the world started out whole, with no pain, suffering, or death. Everything was in perfect balance. But then came a pivotal moment—the Fall. That’s when disorder and decay entered the picture, leaving a mark on every part of creation. In this view, disease isn’t part of the original plan; it’s more like a symptom of something that went wrong.
This isn’t just a story for Sunday mornings. It actually shapes the way we look at the evidence all around us.
If you shift to a biological perspective, you’ll find that many diseases trace back to systems that once worked beautifully. Take bacteria, for example. Some strains are harmful, but their close relatives help us digest food or recycle nutrients in the environment. The problem starts when these microbes lose their natural controls, or when changes in their surroundings give them a chance to go rogue.
The immune system is another case in point. It’s supposed to defend us, but sometimes it gets things wrong—attacking our own tissues, or missing real threats. These aren’t signs that the system is getting better. Instead, they show the difficulties that come when something designed for good starts to break down.
Think about how many pathogens seem to take advantage of what’s already there, rather than inventing new ways to cause trouble. New diseases often pop up when human actions—like changing the environment or moving into new areas—expose weak spots in our defenses. So, instead of creating something brand new, these microbes exploit the gaps left by a world that’s not quite as it should be.
Here are the big ideas to keep in mind:
First, the Fall is seen as a turning point. Disease and death aren’t original features—they’re consequences of a fundamental shift in how creation works.
Second, degeneration and loss play a huge role. Many illnesses come from systems that used to help us but have now broken down.
And third, the choices we make—how we live, what environments we disrupt—can speed up the spread or arrival of disease by upsetting natural balances.
When you put this all together, it encourages us to look at disease through a wider lens. It’s not just about biology, but also about a story—a story of a world in need of restoration.
Instead of seeing suffering and death as necessary steps forward, this framework invites us to imagine hope—hope rooted in the idea that renewal and restoration are possible, even in a world that’s been marked by brokenness.
